subject: English
topic: Error Spotting — Grammatical Errors in Sentences (Set W7)

questions.stem:
Find the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, choose D.

'She (A) don't know (B) anything about (C) the accident. (D) No error'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'She don't know' is wrong. 'She' is third-person singular, so the auxiliary must be 'doesn't': 'She DOESN'T know'. Rule: with he/she/it, use doesn't (not don't) in the present tense.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'Neither the captain (A) nor the players (B) were responsible (C) for the defeat. (D) No error'
questions.explanation: D is correct. The sentence has NO error. With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (the nearer subject rule). Here, 'the players' (plural) is closer to the verb → 'were' is correct. Trap: many students incorrectly change 'were' to 'was' (agreeing with 'the captain' instead).

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'The news about (A) the factory accidents (B) were quite (C) shocking. (D) No error'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'News' is an uncountable singular noun in English — it always takes a singular verb. 'Were' should be 'WAS': 'The news...WAS quite shocking.' Similar nouns: information, advice, furniture, luggage — all singular despite appearing plural.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'Having not studied (A) for the examination, (B) the results (C) disappointed him greatly. (D) No error'

options.option_text: Part A — Having not studied for the examination

questions.explanation: A is correct. Dangling modifier error. 'Having not studied for the examination' must logically modify the person who didn't study — but the sentence's main subject is 'the results', not a person. Correct: 'Having not studied for the examination, HE was disappointed by the results.' Alternatively: 'Not having studied for the exam, he found the results disappointing.'

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'The principal, (A) along with several teachers, (B) are planning (C) a school cultural event. (D) No error'

options.option_text: Part A — The principal, along with several teachers
Part C — a school cultural event

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Along with', 'together with', 'as well as' do NOT create a compound subject — the grammatical subject remains 'The principal' (singular). Verb must be singular: 'IS planning'. 'Are' (plural) is wrong here. Rule: these parenthetical phrases add information but don't change subject-verb agreement.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'I have been living (A) in this city (B) since (C) three years. (D) No error'

options.option_text: Part A — I have been living

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Since' is used for a specific point in time (since 2020, since Monday). 'For' is used for a duration (for three years). 'Three years' is a duration → use 'FOR three years'. Correct: 'I have been living in this city FOR three years.'

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'If I was (A) you, I would (B) have accepted (C) the job offer. (D) No error'

options.option_text: Part A — If I was you
Part C — have accepted the job offer

questions.explanation: A is correct. In hypothetical/unreal conditions (something contrary to fact), English uses the subjunctive mood. 'If I were you' (not 'was') is the correct form. The subjunctive uses 'were' for all persons — I/he/she/we in unreal conditions. 'Was' is indicative; 'were' is subjunctive.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'He is one of those managers (A) who always (B) insists (C) on punctuality. (D) No error'
questions.explanation: B is correct. In 'one of those managers WHO...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'managers' (plural). The verb in the relative clause must be plural: 'who always INSIST'. 'Insists' (singular) wrongly refers to 'one' instead of 'managers'. Correct: 'He is one of those managers who always INSIST on punctuality.'

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'The committee (A) has not reached (B) a consensus (C) on the issue yet. (D) No error'

options.option_text: Part C — a consensus on the issue yet

questions.explanation: D is correct. The sentence has NO error. 'The committee has not reached a consensus' — collective nouns like 'committee', 'team', 'jury' take singular verbs in Indian English ('has', not 'have'). 'Yet' correctly goes with present perfect tense. All parts are grammatically sound.

questions.stem:
Find the part with a grammatical error, or choose D if there is none.

'In spite of (A) working very hardly, (B) she could not (C) clear the interview. (D) No error'

options.option_text: Part C — she could not clear the interview

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Hardly' is an adverb meaning 'barely/almost not' — it is NOT the adverb form of 'hard'. The adverb of 'hard' (as in working with effort) IS 'hard': 'she worked hard'. 'Hardly' means something almost did not happen. Correct: 'working very hard'. 'Working very hardly' is doubly wrong — 'hardly' contradicts the intended meaning.
